what: Rush Enterprises sells and services commercial trucks. It runs the largest network of heavy-duty truck dealerships in the United States, selling new and used trucks, and — more importantly — servicing and repairing them and selling the parts.
customers: Trucking companies, construction firms, municipalities and owner-operators buying, servicing and repairing commercial vehicles across a national dealership network.
money: Heavy and medium-duty trucks, the largest revenue line and the thinnest margin.
Repairs, maintenance and parts, by far the highest-margin business.
Financing and leasing arranged on the vehicles sold.
moat: A truck off the road costs its owner money every hour, so a national network of service locations near the major freight routes is worth paying for. That network is the asset: it produces recurring parts and service revenue from trucks already sold, and it cannot be replicated without decades of dealership agreements and property.
risks: Free cash flow of only $59.4M against $276.6M of net income, because truck inventory financing dominates the cash flow statement.
New truck demand is one of the most cyclical things in the American economy, and it has been in a downturn: revenue fell from $7.9B in 2023 to $7.4B in 2025.
Last year’s net margin was 3.5%, which is the structural reality of vehicle retailing.
Freight rates have been weak, which reduces trucking company profitability and therefore truck purchases.
Only four analysts cover the stock, so the $54.00 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Parts and service is about 35% of revenue and a far larger share of profit, and it depends on trucks on the road rather than trucks being sold.
The shares trade at about 19.4 times earnings, 8.4 times EV/EBITDA and 0.69 times sales.
Debt of $401.9M against $212.6M of cash is modest once floor plan financing is understood.
The national service network is a genuine scale advantage that regional dealers cannot match.
An ageing truck fleet means more repair work, which supports the high-margin business when new sales are weak.
watch: Parts and service revenue, separately from truck sales. The service business is the quality asset; truck sales are the cycle.
view: Truck dealerships are far better businesses than car dealerships, and the reason is downtime. A commercial truck that is not moving costs its owner money every hour, so a trucking company will pay for fast repair near the route it runs. That makes the service network the valuable asset, not the showroom — and Rush has the largest such network in the country, which is a position built over decades of dealership agreements and real estate that nobody can assemble quickly.

The financial statements obscure this. Revenue of $7.5 billion at a 3.5% net margin tells you most of that figure is the cost of trucks passing through. Free cash flow of $59 million against $277 million of net income is inventory financing, not operating weakness. Neither number describes the business. Parts and service is roughly 35% of revenue and a much larger share of profit, and it is the only part worth building a view on.

The cycle is currently against them. New truck orders are among the most cyclical things in the American economy — trucking companies buy when freight rates are strong and stop entirely when they are not — and freight has been weak. Revenue fell from $7.9 billion to $7.4 billion. That is the normal pattern and it will turn, though nobody can say when.

What makes the downturn tolerable is the counter-effect in the service business: when trucking companies cannot afford new trucks, they keep the old ones running, which means more repair work at better margins. That is a genuine internal hedge and it is why this business holds up better through a freight recession than the revenue line suggests. At 8.4 times EV/EBITDA with modest debt, the price is reasonable for a cyclical with a good quality core. Parts and service revenue is the number to follow; truck sales are the weather.
bull: An ageing fleet drives high-margin service work through the freight downturn, then new truck orders recover on top of it, at 8.4 times EV/EBITDA.
bear: The freight recession drags on, truck buyers stay away for years, and a 3.5% margin retailer sees even service volumes fall as fleets shrink.
